 Inspiration 

 As an independent AI consultant working with small businesses across Chile and 
Latin America, I kept running into the same wall: entrepreneurs know they need 
AI agents for their business, but the gap between "I need an agent" and "I have 
a working agent" feels impossibly technical. Meanwhile, most agent-building 
demos are static — they describe what an agent could do instead of letting 
you build one. Fábrica de Agentes de IA started from a simple question: what if 
the landing page itself was the product demo, and visitors could co-create a 
real agent with it in real time, live in the browser? 

 What it does 

 Fábrica de Agentes de IA is an interactive web experience where visitors build 
a micro-agent for their own project step by step: they choose their business 
domain (services, e-commerce, accounting, freelance work), describe the problem 
they want the agent to solve, and the page — powered by WebMCP — exposes tools 
that an LLM calls directly to generate a working system prompt plus a technical 
card summarizing the agent's role, suggested tools, and stack. Visitors leave 
with something tangible they can actually use, not just a description of what's 
possible. 

 How we built it 

 The site is deployed on Netlify and built around WebMCP, which lets the page 
expose browser-side tools that an LLM can invoke directly — turning the landing 
page into an agentic surface rather than a static UI. The generation flow calls 
an LLM to produce the system prompt and technical card in a consistent, 
structured format, following the same "technical card" pattern I'd already 
developed for an internal agent-cataloging project. The interaction was 
designed with two paths in mind: a guided UI for visitors clicking through 
forms, and a direct MCP-client path for anyone who wants to connect their own 
agent straight to the page's exposed tools. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting WebMCP to expose tools cleanly — reliable enough for both a human 
clicking buttons and an external MCP client calling them directly — took more 
iteration than expected, since both paths needed to hit the same underlying 
tool calls without diverging behavior. Prompt design was the other major 
challenge: getting the LLM to consistently return a well-structured technical 
card (not just freeform text) across very different business domains, without 
the output feeling generic or copy-pasted between users. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting a genuinely functional live demo working — not a mockup — where a 
visitor can go from "I run a small accounting firm" to a usable system prompt 
in under a few minutes. Also proud of making the page dual-purpose: it works as 
a simple, approachable builder for non-technical visitors, while still being a 
real demonstration of WebMCP's agentic capabilities for a technical audience. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP genuinely changes what a landing page can be — it stops being a static 
pitch and becomes a live capability surface. I also learned a lot about the gap 
between "an LLM can generate a system prompt" and "an LLM can generate a 
 consistently structured, production-ready system prompt" — the latter needed 
much more careful prompt engineering than I initially expected. 

 What's next for Fábrica de Agentes de IA 

 Next steps are connecting the generated agents to a "request production 
version" flow tied to my AI consulting practice, adding domain-specific 
templates informed by real client work in the Chilean SME market, and exploring 
multi-agent orchestration so visitors can co-create a small team of agents 
instead of just one. I'd also like to open the page to accept connections from 
external MCP clients more broadly, so it becomes a reusable building block 
other developers can plug into, not just a standalone demo.
